translation_en: And what does it matter that Albert is your husband? Husband! Then, for this world—and in the eyes of this world—it would be a sin that **I love you**, that I should wish to tear you from his arms into mine? A sin? Good, and I punish myself for it; I have tasted this sin in all its heavenly bliss, have drawn balm of life and strength from it into my heart. From this moment on you are mine! Mine, O Lotte! I go on ahead! I go to my Father, to your Father. To him I will pour out my grief, and he will comfort me until you come; then I shall fly to meet you and clasp you and remain with you before the face of the Infinite in eternal embraces.
larger_context_summary: Werther addresses Lotte in a final written outpouring shortly before his suicide. Lotte is married to Albert, whose pistols Werther has arranged to borrow, ostensibly for a journey but in fact for his death. After Werther’s increasingly intrusive passion and a charged final encounter with Lotte, she has imposed separation. Here he rejects the worldly authority of her marriage and imagines death as going ahead of her to their shared divine Father, where an eternal union will supersede social and marital barriers. Lotte does not share his possessive certainty, and the stakes are therefore not a mutual romantic future but Werther’s fatal reinterpretation of rejection, guilt, and suicide as punishment, transcendence, and reunion.
interpretive_commentary: The love clause is embedded within a rhetorical question about whether loving Lotte counts as a worldly sin. That embedding does not weaken its truth commitment: Werther disputes the moral classification, not the reality, of his love. The exceptionally high truth-conditional force is therefore apt. By contrast, the clause itself does not create a promise, vow, or reciprocal bond; the possessive declaration “you are mine” and fantasy of eternal embraces occur elsewhere in the passage and cannot make the target expression performative. Nor should emotional extremity automatically count as expressive or reflexive force. Werther’s repetition, exclamations, and eschatological imagery make the surrounding address feverishly intense, but “I love you” remains grammatically controlled evidence within an argument. The case is valuable precisely because it separates semantic avowal from dramatic excess: even in a deceptive and suicidal final letter, the relevant deception concerns his plans, not his stated love.
